background: Twenty moves are legal from the initial position: two for each of the eight pawns and two for each knight. Four of them, 1.e4, 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4, are by far the most popular and the ones worth learning. The rest are rated here so that every first move gets a verdict, but only the good ones are followed further.

1.e4.strategy: Claims a central square at once and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, so White can develop quickly and castle early. The price is a pawn that no other pawn defends, so Black can challenge it right away; the game tends to open early and can turn sharp.

1.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn that the queen already defends, so Black has no quick target, and opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop. It also fights for c5 and e5. The game tends to stay closed longer, and the struggle is about space and pawn structure more than early tactics.

1.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e5 and d4 without committing a pawn, so White can still choose later between a pawn centre, a fianchetto set-up or a quiet build-up. It also rules out ...e5, which would simply lose the pawn. The cost is that White shows little and lets Black make the first big decision.

1.c4.strategy: Fights for d5 from the side and leaves the central pawns at home, so White decides later between building a pawn centre and a fianchetto set-up. Flexible and solid, often with asymmetrical positions when Black takes the centre with a pawn. It develops no piece and does not yet free the king's bishop, so development starts a move later.

1.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which then watches the long diagonal and supports a later push in the centre. The move commits nothing there, and the game usually becomes a closed, manoeuvring one with that bishop. The risk is that Black takes central space unchallenged.

1.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which then eyes e5 and presses along the long diagonal on Black's kingside. White lets Black build a pawn centre on purpose and plans to undermine it later; the price is the central space Black gets meanwhile.

1.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and prepares an attack on the kingside, at the price of weakening it: the e1–h4 diagonal is open, and the move does nothing for development. The game is unbalanced, a bet that the attack outweighs that risk.

1.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and watches d5 and e4 without weakening anything. But it blocks the c-pawn, which White often wants to push, and does not stop Black from taking the centre; ...d5 followed by ...d4 can even chase the knight. Playable, yet a less effective use of the first move than the main ones.

1.b4.strategy: Gains space on the queenside and prepares Bb2 against e5 and g7. It shows White's plan before Black has shown anything, the pawn on b4 can become a target, and Black simply takes the centre. Rare at the top level.

1.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and keeps every option open, since it can transpose into many openings. On its own it claims little: the e-pawn goes only one step, the queen's bishop stays shut in, and White gives up most of the first-move advantage.

1.d3.name: Mieses Opening
1.d3.background: Named after Jacques Mieses, who used it in his 1910 match against Teichmann. Deep Blue played it against Kasparov in the third game of their 1997 match, which was drawn.
1.d3.strategy: Covers e4 and opens the queen's bishop, a modest claim to the centre. White aims for a flexible set-up with a fianchettoed king's bishop, but it is slow: Black can occupy the centre and take the initiative.

1.c3.name: Saragossa Opening
1.c3.background: Became popular at the Saragossa chess club in 1919; the next year the club member José Juncosa analysed it, and in 1922 a thematic tournament in Mannheim, won by Tarrasch, required the players to open with it.
1.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 backed by a pawn and keeps the structure solid, but it takes c3 from the knight and claims the centre only timidly. Not bad, but the main first moves do more.

1.a3.name: Anderssen's Opening
1.a3.background: Named after Adolf Anderssen, who played it three times against Paul Morphy in their Paris match of December 1858, scoring 1½ out of 3. Steinitz, Blackburne and Mieses tried it later, and Nakamura beat Carlsen with it in an online blitz game in 2023.
1.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it controls b4 and keeps every piece at home, so Black must show a plan first. It does little for development or the centre and hands the first-move advantage to Black, who in effect plays White.

1.h3.name: Clemenz Opening
1.h3.background: Named after Hermann Clemenz (1846–1908), an Estonian player. Among the rarest first moves; Michael Basman has experimented with it as a prelude to 2.g4 or 2.a3.
1.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's pieces and nothing more: it claims no central square, develops nothing, and slightly weakens the kingside where White usually castles. A tempo spent for later, like 1.a3.

1.g4.strategy: Grabs space on the kingside and prepares Bg2 on the long diagonal, hoping for an unprepared opponent. The pawn on g4 is undefended, the kingside is weakened for good, and Black takes the centre. Widely considered one of the worst first moves.

1.f3.name: Barnes Opening
1.f3.background: Named after Thomas Wilson Barnes (1825–1874), the English player who scored eight wins against Paul Morphy in 1858, one of them with 1.e4 f6 as Black. Edmar Mednis argued that 1.f3 is the worst of the twenty first moves.
1.f3.strategy: Covers e4 and nothing else: it develops no piece, opens no line, takes the knight's best square f3 and opens the e1–h4 diagonal against White's uncastled king. Almost any other move serves the same aim better.

1.h4.strategy: Gains space on the kingside and threatens h5 against a fianchetto, but does nothing for the centre or development, and the rook rarely comes out via h3. The side where White usually castles is weakened, and the pawn cannot go back.

1.a4.strategy: Attacks b5 and prepares to bring the rook out via a3, but b5 matters to nobody, and after 1...e5 the bishop on f8 keeps the rook in. A lost tempo that ignores the centre entirely.

1.Na3.strategy: A knight on the rim controls no central square, and once Black has moved the e-pawn the bishop from f8 can take it and double White's pawns. White gives up most of the first-move advantage; a later c4 or e4 may still reach a reasonable position.

1.Nh3.name: Amar Opening
1.Nh3.background: Named after Charles Amar, a Parisian amateur who played it in the 1930s, probably by Tartakower, who also called it the Paris Opening. Carlsen beat Dreev with it in a 2018 online rapid game.
1.Nh3.strategy: The knight on h3 has little future: it reaches only f4 and g5, and 1...d5 already threatens ...Bxh3, which would double White's pawns on the kingside. Black takes the centre undisturbed.

1.a3 e5.strategy: The natural answer to a waiting move: Black claims the centre at once and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop. White's pawn on a3 does nothing yet to contest the centre, so Black has a comfortable game and White has to decide how to fight for the squares.

1.a3 a5.strategy: Answers a rim-pawn move with a rim-pawn move, meant to keep White's b-pawn from advancing. It does nothing for the centre or for development, so Black spends a tempo on stopping a plan White may never follow.

1.a3 d5.strategy: Takes space in the centre at once, and the pawn on a3 does nothing to challenge it. Black gets a solid, flexible set-up in which White, having spent the first move on the rim, is the side that has to find a way to fight for the centre.

1.a3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and watches the e4 and d5 squares without committing a pawn. Black lets White show what the extra move on a3 is for and keeps every set-up available, at the price of not yet claiming any space.

1.a3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle early, controlling the centre from a distance. The bishop on g7 would contest the long diagonal before White's queen's bishop can settle there, but the pawn centre is left to White if Black is slow.

1.a3 a5 2.b4.name: Anderssen's Opening: Polish Gambit
1.a3 a5 2.b4.strategy: A dubious gambit: the pawn is offered to open the long diagonal for the bishop and the a-file for the rook. Black simply takes it, and White cannot retake with the a-pawn, because the rook on a8 would then capture the rook on a1. The open lines are not worth a pawn.

1.a3 a5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and puts the extra tempo to use. Black's a5 helps neither development nor the centre, so White can build a broad pawn centre and develop freely while Black has to catch up.

1.a3 a5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with the queen's pawn and opens the diagonal of the queen's bishop, keeping the choice between a slow build-up and quicker play. Slightly less direct than the king's pawn, since the pawn needs support from the pieces, but it likewise profits from Black's wasted move.

1.a3 a5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and commits no pawn, so every set-up stays open. White simply makes use of the tempo Black has wasted, at the cost of leaving Black the chance to take a central square first.

1.a3 e5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares to put the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it eyes the e5 pawn and the kingside. White leaves the centre to Black for now and plays for pressure from a distance, a slow but sound set-up.

1.a3 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle early, aiming at the long diagonal. White accepts that Black has the larger share of the centre and plays a flexible, quiet game, hoping to undermine the pawn on e5 later.

1.a3 e5 2.Nc3.name: Dunst Opening: Battambang Variation
1.a3 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a knight towards the centre, where it eyes the e4 and d5 squares, and the pawn on a3 takes the b4 square away from Black's bishop. The cost is that the knight blocks the c-pawn, so White cannot build the c4 set-up and leaves the centre to Black.

1.a3 e5 2.c4.strategy: Fights for the d5 square from the flank, and here the pawn on a3 is a useful extra move: it covers b4, so Black's bishop cannot use that square, and it prepares a queenside advance. Black holds the larger share of the centre, but White gets a flexible strategic game in which the extra move counts.

1.a3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Meets Black's central pawn with its own and aims for an open, symmetrical game in which the pawn on a3 earns its place: it takes b4 away from Black's bishop, so the bishop cannot attack a knight on c3 from there. The price is the tempo already spent on the rim, so White has no real edge.

1.d3 e5.name: Mieses Opening: Reversed Rat
1.d3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre at once, since White's modest first move has left it free. Black gets a full pawn on e5 and easy development, and White has to prove that the flexible, less committal set-up is worth the space it concedes.

1.d3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which will press on the long diagonal against White's queenside. Black leaves the centre to White for now and relies on solid development and a later counter-strike, a sound set-up against a first move that claims little.

1.d3 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre from the flank and prepares to meet White's slow set-up with queenside play. Black keeps the choice between a quick ...e5 and a more restrained plan, at the price of a less direct hold on the centre than the e-pawn gives.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight where it eyes the d5 and e4 squares and keeps the position flexible. The c-pawn is blocked, so White settles for a restrained set-up with a kingside fianchetto instead of a quick central break.

1.d3 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight eyes d4 and e5, so Black's central advances are met at once, and White commits no further pawn. The position stays flexible and White aims for a quiet game in which development, not early pawn tension, sets the course.

1.d3 c5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which has no future on f1 behind the d3-pawn but a long diagonal on g2. White aims for a slow, compact set-up with the king safe and the centre challenged later; the price is that Black can claim space in the middle first.

1.d3 c5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre with the e-pawn, backed by d3, and builds a sturdy pawn chain. It is sound but modest: the d3-pawn keeps the f1-bishop shut in, and Black's c-pawn already pulls at the d4 square, so White has little more than a solid, slower game.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds a second guard to d4, so White cannot easily claim that square. Black mirrors White's flexible set-up and keeps every option open for the centre.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on e4 and d5, so any central advance by White has to reckon with it. Black keeps the pawn structure flexible and can still choose between a fianchetto and a central build-up.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which then looks along the long diagonal at the c3-knight and the b2-pawn. Black plays for a solid kingside and pressure on the queenside, letting White decide how to use the centre.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Grabs the centre with a second pawn and a firm grip on d4, but with the c-pawn already on c5 nothing guards d5, so the c3-knight can head there at once. Black gets space at the price of a weak d5.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.name: Mieses Opening: Venezolana Variation
1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, which has little to do on f1 behind the d3-pawn but a long diagonal to rule from g2. White aims at a slow, solid game in which the bishop and the knight on c3 together pressure d5 and the queenside.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Brings out the second knight, which now guards d4 and e5 before White decides what to do with the pawns. A flexible, low-risk set-up: the cost is that it commits to no plan, so Black can choose the pawn structure.

1.d3 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.e4.strategy: Builds a pawn centre at once, with e4 backed by d3 and the knight on c3, and takes d5 away from Black's pieces. The f1-bishop stays hemmed in behind the pawns, so White plays a slow build-up on the kingside rather than for a quick break.

1.d3 e5 2.Nd2.name: Valencia Opening
1.d3 e5 2.Nd2.strategy: Heads for the centre with the knight and leaves the f-pawn free, but it shuts in the queen's bishop and cramps development. The move is playable, since that bishop can still come out on b2 after b3, but it is the less natural way to answer Black's central pawn.

1.d3 e5 2.c4.strategy: The most accurate way to meet the centre pawn: it controls d5, takes space on the queenside, and lets the b1-knight reach c3 without blocking a c-pawn. White gets the English set-up with the pawn already on d3, a flexible game in which the centre is fought over from the flank.

1.d3 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on e5 while the pawn on d3 covers e4, so Black cannot push the e-pawn forward to drive the knight away. White gets a comfortable, harmonious development and keeps every set-up available.

1.d3 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, which the d3-pawn would otherwise keep shut in. White settles for a compact, patient game with a safe king and a later challenge to Black's centre.

1.d3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Matches Black's central pawn and keeps the position symmetrical and level. It is sound but gives Black no problems: the f1-bishop is blocked by the d3-pawn, and White has little way to play for more than equality.

1.d3 g6 2.g4.name: Mieses Opening: Myers Spike Attack
1.d3 g6 2.g4.strategy: A flank thrust that grabs space on the kingside and prepares to push the pawns further. It loosens White's own king's side before a single piece has moved, so the attack must justify itself quickly; Black gets a free hand in the centre meanwhile.

1.d3 g6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre while Black's pieces are still at home: the e4-pawn, backed by d3, controls d5 and f5 and gives White more space. Black's bishop, once fianchettoed, must then work against a solid centre, and White can build up at leisure.

1.d3 g6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to its best square, where it covers d4 and e5, and keeps the choice of centre open. A sound, flexible move that makes no commitment and lets White see how Black sets up.

1.d3 g6 2.c4.strategy: Claims space on the queenside and the d5 square, a flank set-up that restrains Black's centre from a distance. It is playable but slower than occupying the centre, and the d3-pawn still blocks the f1-bishop.

1.f3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, aiming at the e1–h4 diagonal that White's first move has weakened. Black develops with ease while White has spent a tempo on a move that develops nothing and takes the knight's natural square.

1.f3 d5.strategy: Claims a share of the centre with the d-pawn and frees the queen's bishop, a sound reply that gives White no target. It is less pointed than the e-pawn, which aims straight at the weakened diagonal, but Black still has the easier game.

1.f3 f5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and stakes a claim to e4. It is playable, but it fights for the centre only indirectly and opens the e8–h5 diagonal against Black's own king, so Black passes up the simple central development that White's first move allows.

1.f3 d5 2.e4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and offers a pawn trade. It undoes part of the damage of the first move, but the pawn on f3 still takes the knight's natural square and leaves the king on an open diagonal, so Black has an easy game.

1.f3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Takes space in the centre with a pawn that needs no help from f3, matching Black's own pawn. It is the sound way to go on: White builds a classical centre and keeps the e-pawn flexible, accepting that f3 has cost the king's knight its natural square and left the king's diagonal open.

1.f3 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece with pressure on d5 and prepares e4 with the knight's support. The knight blocks the c-pawn and can be driven back by Black's d-pawn, so White gets a playable but passive game that has no clear plan.

1.f3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Puts a pawn in the centre and frees the queen and the king's bishop, as 1.e4 would have done without the weakening move. It is the most direct repair, though the pawn on f3 still takes the knight's natural square and leaves the e1-h4 diagonal open, so Black keeps the easier game.

1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.name: Barnes Opening: Hammerschlag
1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.background: In 2020 Magnus Carlsen played 2.Kf2 against Wesley So in a blitz game. So said it was humiliating when someone plays f3 and Kf2 and just crushes you.
1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.strategy: A provocation rather than a plan: the king gives up castling and steps onto the open diagonal, where ...Qh4+ and ...Bc5+ are both check at once. Black only has to develop sensibly and make use of the exposed king.

1.f3 e5 2.g4.strategy: Walks into the fastest possible mate: 2...Qh4# ends the game on the spot, because the pawns on f3 and g4 have opened the diagonal to the king and nothing can block it or give the king a square.

1.f3 e5 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the knight to the only square f3 leaves it. On the rim it eyes little and can be traded off by the c8-bishop, which would double White's h-pawns. Black takes the centre at leisure against a cramped, passive set-up.

1.f3 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and offers a pawn to open the game. With f3 taking the knight's square, White cannot recapture on d4 with a piece but only with the queen, which Black then drives about with gain of time while the king's diagonal stays open.

1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.name: Barnes Opening: Fool's Mate
1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.background: The fool's mate was named and described in The Royal Game of Chess-Play, a 1656 text by Francis Beale that adapted the work of Gioachino Greco. It is the fastest checkmate in chess, and it can occur only if White commits an extraordinary blunder.
1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.strategy: Checkmate on the second move. The queen reaches h4 along the diagonal that f3 and g4 have opened, the king has no flight square, and no White piece can interpose or capture the queen.

1.f3 e5 2.g4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre and keeps the threat of ...Qh4# alive, but passes up the checkmate that is on the board. White gets one move to meet the threat, and Black has to win the slower way. Black stays far ahead, but the win is no longer forced.

1.f3 e5 2.g4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps ...Qh4# in hand, but again passes up the mate on the board. The knight adds nothing to the attack along the king's diagonal, so White gets time to cover it, and Black has to convert a large advantage the long way.

1.f3 f5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre and invites the exchange: after ...fxe4 the recapture with the f-pawn restores the material and leaves White a pawn on e4 and a knight free to use its natural square. It undoes the damage of the first move more fully than quiet development, and the game is roughly level.

1.f3 f5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and keeps e4 for later, once pieces are out to support it. It does not fight for e4 at once, so Black chooses the set-up, but White's position is sound: f3 has cost the knight its square and the king's diagonal needs watching, little more.

1.f3 f5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares e4 with the knight's support. It blocks the c-pawn and lets Black choose the set-up first, with f3 still keeping the other knight from its natural square, so White's game is playable but passive.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes White's central pawn. White regains it with the f-pawn, so material is level again, White has a pawn on e4 and the f-file is open for both sides. Black has the easier development and is not worse, but not a pawn up either.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 d6.strategy: Opens the bishop's diagonal so that exf5 can be met by ...Bxf5, which keeps material level with a developed piece. Black avoids the open lines of the exchange on e4, but gives White the choice and leaves White the extra space in the centre.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 e6.strategy: Prepares to recapture on f5 with the e-pawn, so Black keeps material level without taking on e4. It releases the tension and leaves Black a solid but passive pawn on f5, while the e-file opens for both uncastled kings.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3.name: Barnes Opening: Gedult Gambit
1.f3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: Attacks the pawn on e4 a second time and develops a piece. Black can keep the pawn by taking on f3, leaving White only quick development to show for it, so this is a gambit that White has to justify; recapturing at once is simpler.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.fxe4.strategy: The simple recapture: material is level again, White has a pawn on e4 and the knight on g1 finally has f3 to use. The f-pawns are gone, so the f-file is open for both sides. It repairs the damage of the first move better than any other, and the game is roughly even.

1.f3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre first and leaves the pawn on e4 for the moment. Black can keep the extra pawn by taking on f3, and White then plays for the lead in development with little more than open lines to show for it.

1.h3 e5.strategy: The natural reply: a central pawn that frees the queen and the king's bishop and takes d4 and f4 away from White. White's first move did nothing for the centre or development, so plain developing moves give Black a slight edge.

1.h3 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop, which now eyes the h3 pawn. White's first move has not helped any plan, so Black develops freely with a freer game.

1.h3 h5.strategy: Copies White's slow first move instead of using the free tempo. It does nothing for the centre or development and loosens Black's own kingside pawns, so Black gives away the easy edge that White's waiting move offered.

1.h3 d5 2.a3.strategy: A second move on the rim, aimed at a quick c4 against the d5 pawn and at keeping a black bishop off b4. It is sound but passive: Black keeps the freer centre.

1.h3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with a second pawn and opens the c1-bishop, so White gets a quiet, solid game in which the spare h3 costs little. The pawn controls e5 and c5 and leaves White free to choose how to develop; the middlegame is positional, with no early forcing play.

1.h3 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight toward the centre while h3 already takes g4 from Black's bishop, so the pin ...Bg4 is not available. White keeps the pawn structure flexible and plays a patient game; Black has the easier time in the centre but no real target to aim at.

1.h3 d5 2.a3 e5.name: Creepy Crawly Formation: Classical Defence
1.h3 d5 2.a3 e5.strategy: Adds a second central pawn, so Black owns a broad centre while White has spent two moves on the edge pawns. White now has to show that the flank set-up is worth the lost time, and Black can simply develop and play for the centre.

1.h3 d5 2.a3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds control of e4 while the d5 pawn holds the centre. Black commits no further pawn, so the game stays flexible, and White's two rim-pawn moves have given Black a comfortable lead in development.

1.h3 d5 2.a3 c5.strategy: Contests the d4 square from the wing, so White cannot build a pawn centre unchallenged. It is sound but more a flank plan than a central one: Black gains queenside space while the e-pawn stays at home and the centre is less fully occupied.

1.h3 e5 2.a3.name: Global Opening
1.h3 e5 2.a3.background: Also known as the Creepy Crawly Formation, a humorous name for the formation of White's wing pawns.
1.h3 e5 2.a3.strategy: Stays on the wing for the second move in a row, preparing a quick c4 and a slow build-up while stopping a black bishop from coming to b4. Black already holds the centre, so White plays a patient game from a passive position.

1.h3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Occupies the centre at once and turns the game into an open game with the colours reversed: h3 takes g4 from Black's bishop and rules out ...Bg4. White is a tempo down on the usual open game but the extra move is not useless, and the play is classical and open.

1.h3 e5 2.c4.strategy: Fights for the d5 square from the flank and keeps the d- and e-pawns flexible. It is a patient plan in which Black holds the centre and White works against it with piece pressure, and h3 may later support a g4 advance.

1.h3 h5 2.g4.name: Clemenz Opening: Spike Lee Gambit
1.h3 h5 2.g4.background: Its association with the filmmaker Spike Lee probably has no direct connection. No tournament game with the gambit is on record.
1.h3 h5 2.g4.strategy: Gives a pawn away for nothing: 2...hxg4 wins it, and 3.hxg4 would open the h-file for 3...Rxh1, winning the rook. White's kingside is left loose and there is no compensation for the pawn.

1.h3 h5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre and develops freely: Black's last move did nothing for development or the centre and loosened the kingside, so White can simply follow the standard principles and stand better.

1.h3 h5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with the d-pawn and opens the c1-bishop. It is a solid, quieter way to punish the useless h5, though it leaves the e-pawn at home and so builds the centre a little less quickly.

1.Nh3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and punishes the knight's odd square: ...Bxh3 threatens to take it and double White's kingside pawns. Black loses nothing by being the first to occupy the centre, and White has to spend a move on the knight's problem.

1.Nh3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre but does not threaten the knight, so the knight's odd square is simply left to White's conscience. Black gets a solid centre pawn and a free development, and White, a tempo behind, has to find a plan for a knight that does nothing for the centre.

1.Nh3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight to the square from which it eyes d4 and e5, so White cannot build a centre unopposed. Sound and flexible, but it blocks the c-pawn and takes no space in the centre, as ...e5 or ...d5 do.

1.Nh3 Nf6.strategy: A natural developing move that keeps an eye on e4 and d5 and so hinders White's own centre. It leaves the centre pawns for later and gives up the immediate pressure on the knight, so White gets time to sort out the kingside.

1.Nh3 d5 2.g3.strategy: The usual answer to the threat: after ...Bxh3 the bishop takes back, so White's pawns stay whole. The move also opens the long diagonal for the king's bishop. The knight remains on the rim and White a tempo behind, so the game is a slow one in which Black has the easier time.

1.Nh3 d5 2.Nf4.strategy: Rescues the knight from the rim before the doubled pawns can come and aims it at d5. The square is not stable, though: ...e5 kicks the knight at once and Black gains time and space in the centre.

1.Nh3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Lets Black take the knight and ruin the kingside pawns, in return for the two bishops, a half-open g-file for the rook and a pawn in the centre. White has real activity, but the broken structure remains a lasting weakness.
